subject: biology
title: Human evolution
summary: How hominins are classified, the trends of bipedalism, larger brains and tool use, key hominin species, and the fossil and DNA evidence for human evolution and migration.
body:
Humans are one twig on a large, bushy family tree of species that walked upright. Fossils, tools and ancient DNA let us trace how our lineage changed after it split from the ancestors of chimpanzees. This story also explains features of our own bodies, from our arched feet to our large brains.

## Key ideas

### Where humans fit: classification

Humans are classified in a nested series of groups, each defined by shared features inherited from a common ancestor.

| Group | Who is included | Key shared features |
|---|---|---|
| **Mammals** | all mammals | hair, mammary glands, three middle ear bones |
| **Primates** | lemurs, monkeys, apes, humans | grasping hands (often feet) with nails, opposable thumbs, forward-facing eyes giving **stereoscopic (3D) vision**, relatively large brains, long period of parental care |
| **Hominoids** (apes) | gibbons, orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos, humans | no tail, more upright posture, flexible shoulder joints, larger brains than monkeys |
| **Hominids** (great apes) | orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos, humans and their extinct relatives | larger body and brain, longer development |
| **Hominins** | modern humans and all extinct species more closely related to us than to chimpanzees | **habitual bipedalism** (walking upright on two legs) |

So a **hominin** is any member of the human lineage after it split from the lineage leading to chimpanzees and bonobos. DNA evidence suggests that split happened roughly 6–7 million years ago. Chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest living relatives; they did not "become" humans. We share a common ancestor with them.

### Trend 1: bipedalism

**Bipedalism** is the feature that defines hominins, and it can be recognised in fossil bones. Compared with a chimpanzee, a bipedal hominin has:

- a **foramen magnum** (the hole where the spinal cord enters the skull) positioned more **centrally underneath** the skull, so the head balances on top of an upright spine
- an **S-shaped spine**, which keeps the centre of gravity over the hips and absorbs shock
- a **short, wide, bowl-shaped pelvis** that supports the organs and anchors muscles for balance when on one leg
- **femurs angled inwards** towards the knees (the carrying angle), placing the feet under the body's centre of gravity
- a **non-opposable big toe** in line with the other toes and an **arched foot**, which acts like a spring when walking
- legs that are long relative to the arms.

Fossilised footprints and leg and pelvis bones show that some early hominins walked upright well before brains became large. Bipedalism may have been favoured because it freed the hands for carrying, allowed a wider view over grassland, and was an energy-efficient way to walk long distances.

### Trend 2: brain size and skull shape

Over time, the hominin lineage shows a general increase in brain size, measured as **cranial capacity** (the volume inside the braincase). Approximate averages:

| Species | Approximate cranial capacity |
|---|---|
| Chimpanzee (for comparison) | about 400 cm³ |
| *Australopithecus* species | about 400–500 cm³ |
| *Homo habilis* | about 600 cm³ |
| *Homo erectus* | about 900–1100 cm³ |
| *Homo sapiens* | about 1350 cm³ |

Along with larger brains came other skull changes:

- a **higher, more rounded braincase** and a vertical forehead
- **smaller brow ridges**
- a **flatter face** with less jutting jaw (reduced **prognathism**)
- **smaller teeth**, especially canines, and a **parabolic (curved) dental arch** instead of the U-shaped arch of apes
- in *Homo sapiens*, a distinct **chin**.

Smaller jaws and teeth are linked to changes in diet and to food processing with tools and, later, cooking.

### Trend 3: tool use and culture

**Culture** means learned behaviour passed between individuals and generations, such as tool-making, language and art. In hominins it became increasingly complex:

- **Simple stone tools** (sharp flakes struck from cobbles, called **Oldowan** tools) are associated with early *Homo*, such as *Homo habilis* ("handy man").
- ***Homo erectus*** made more carefully shaped, symmetrical **hand axes** (Acheulean tools) and is associated with the use of fire, though exactly when fire use began is still debated.
- ***Homo neanderthalensis*** made refined stone tools, used fire, wore simple clothing and buried some of their dead.
- ***Homo sapiens*** developed a wide range of specialised tools, art, ornaments and complex language.

Culture works alongside genetic evolution: tools and fire allowed hominins to get more energy from food and to survive in colder environments.

### Examples of hominin species

- ***Australopithecus afarensis*** – lived in East Africa a little over 3 million years ago; the famous partial skeleton "Lucy" belongs to this species. Bipedal, but with a small, ape-sized brain and long arms suited to climbing.
- ***Homo habilis*** – early member of our genus, with a somewhat larger brain and associated with simple stone tools.
- ***Homo erectus*** – taller with body proportions close to ours, a larger brain, and the first hominin known to have spread out of Africa into Asia.
- ***Homo neanderthalensis*** (Neanderthals) – lived in Europe and western Asia; stocky build suited to cold climates, large brains, prominent brow ridges. They became extinct around 40 000 years ago.
- ***Homo sapiens*** – modern humans, the only hominin species alive today.

The hominin family tree is **bushy, not a ladder**: several hominin species lived at the same time, and many lineages ended without descendants.

### Evidence for human evolution

- **Fossils** – skulls, teeth, pelvises and leg bones show changes in brain size, face shape and bipedalism. Radiometric dating of surrounding volcanic layers gives their ages.
- **Artefacts** – stone tools, hearths and art show changes in behaviour and culture.
- **DNA** – comparisons between living humans and great apes show chimpanzees and bonobos are our closest relatives. **Ancient DNA** extracted from fossil bones has shown that *Homo sapiens* interbred with Neanderthals and with another group called the **Denisovans**, known mainly from DNA. Many people living today carry a small proportion of DNA from these groups.
- **Mitochondrial DNA** – because it is passed down the maternal line, comparisons of mtDNA in living people show the greatest diversity in African populations, supporting an African origin for our species.

### Migration of *Homo sapiens*

Evidence from fossils and DNA supports the **Out of Africa model**: *Homo sapiens* evolved in Africa, and some populations later migrated out of Africa, spreading across Asia, Europe, Australia and eventually the Americas. As they spread, they largely replaced other hominin populations, with some interbreeding.

Key points on timing, in general terms:

- The oldest known *Homo sapiens* fossils come from Africa and are roughly 300 000 years old.
- The main successful dispersal out of Africa is generally placed within the last 100 000 years.
- People reached Australia at least 50 000 years ago, which means Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. Reaching Australia required crossing open sea, showing planning and boat-building.
- The Americas were reached much later.

Exact dates are regularly revised as new finds are made, so treat these as approximate.

The main alternative idea, the **multiregional model**, proposed that modern humans evolved gradually from *Homo erectus* populations in several regions at once, connected by gene flow. The genetic evidence (greatest diversity in Africa) mostly supports the Out of Africa model, while ancient DNA shows a small amount of interbreeding with other hominins.

## Worked examples

### Worked example 1: is this fossil bipedal?

*A skull is found with a foramen magnum located towards the back of the skull. A pelvis from the same site is tall and narrow. Was this individual a habitual biped?*

**Step 1 – foramen magnum:** towards the back means the spine joined the skull at an angle, as in a knuckle-walking ape.
**Step 2 – pelvis:** tall and narrow is ape-like; bipeds have a short, wide, bowl-shaped pelvis.
**Conclusion:** both features suggest this was **not** a habitual biped, so it is unlikely to be a hominin.

### Worked example 2: placing an unknown skull

*A newly found skull has a cranial capacity of about 1000 cm³, large brow ridges, no chin and a moderately flat face. Stone hand axes are found nearby.*

**Step 1 – brain size:** about 1000 cm³ is larger than *Australopithecus* and *H. habilis*, smaller than the *H. sapiens* average.
**Step 2 – features:** large brow ridges and no chin rule out *H. sapiens*.
**Step 3 – tools:** shaped hand axes are associated with *H. erectus*.
**Conclusion:** the evidence fits ***Homo erectus*** best. In an exam, state the features you used and link each to a species.

## Common mistakes

- Saying "humans evolved from chimpanzees". Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor; neither evolved from the other.
- Drawing human evolution as a straight line from one species to the next. Several hominin species coexisted.
- Confusing **hominid** (great apes and humans) with **hominin** (the human lineage only).
- Thinking a big brain came first. Bipedalism evolved well before large brain size.
- Stating precise dates confidently. Dates are estimates and are often revised.

## Exam tips

- Learn the skeletal evidence for bipedalism (foramen magnum, spine, pelvis, femur, foot) and be able to compare a hominin and an ape skeleton.
- For "classify this fossil" questions, use several features (brain size, face, teeth, tools) and justify each.
- Be able to explain how mtDNA and ancient DNA support the Out of Africa model and interbreeding with Neanderthals.
- Define terms precisely: hominoid, hominid, hominin.

## Tips to remember

- **Hominid vs hominin: the "n" means "nearer"** (made-up trick): a homini**n** is in the human lineage only (nearer to us than to chimpanzees); a homini**d** takes in all the great apes as well. Hominoid (with the "o") is the widest group: all apes, including gibbons.
- **Build an upright body from the top down: "Hole, Spine, Hips, Thighs, Feet"** (made-up trick): central foramen magnum → S-shaped spine → short, wide, bowl-shaped pelvis → femurs angled inwards → arched foot with a big toe in line. Run down this checklist on any skeleton question.
- **Feet before brains:** "Lucy" (*Australopithecus afarensis*) walked upright with an ape-sized brain of about 400–500 cm³. Bipedalism came first; big brains (about 1350 cm³ in *Homo sapiens*) came much later.
- **Brain sizes roughly climb in steps of a few hundred:** chimp and *Australopithecus* about 400–500 → *H. habilis* about 600 → *H. erectus* about 900–1100 → *H. sapiens* about 1350 cm³. A skull near 1000 cm³ with big brow ridges, no chin and hand axes nearby points to *H. erectus*.
- **Picture a bush, not a ladder:** several hominin species lived at the same time, and many branches died out. Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees; we share a common ancestor about 6–7 million years ago.
- **Out of Africa self-check:** the greatest mtDNA diversity is in Africa, because the population that has been somewhere longest has had the most time to build up variation. Add "with some interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans" for the full picture.

## Key terms

- **Primate** — mammal with grasping hands, forward-facing eyes and a relatively large brain.
- **Hominoid** — an ape or human; tailless primates.
- **Hominid** — great apes and humans, and their extinct relatives.
- **Hominin** — humans and all extinct species more closely related to us than to chimpanzees.
- **Bipedalism** — habitually walking upright on two legs.
- **Foramen magnum** — the hole in the base of the skull where the spinal cord passes through.
- **Cranial capacity** — the internal volume of the braincase.
- **Prognathism** — the forward projection of the jaw and face.
- **Culture** — learned behaviour passed on between individuals and generations.
- **Out of Africa model** — the idea that *Homo sapiens* evolved in Africa and then migrated, largely replacing other hominins.

## Summary

- Hominins are humans and their extinct relatives after the split from the chimpanzee lineage, defined by bipedalism.
- Skeletal clues to bipedalism include a central foramen magnum, S-shaped spine, bowl-shaped pelvis, angled femurs and arched feet.
- Over time hominins show larger brains, flatter faces, smaller teeth and increasingly complex tools and culture.
- The hominin family tree is bushy, with several species living at the same time.
- Fossils, artefacts, mtDNA and ancient DNA support an African origin of *Homo sapiens*, with later migration and some interbreeding with Neanderthals and Denisovans.

questions.prompt: Which feature is used to define a hominin?
questions.explanation: Hominins are defined by habitual upright walking on two legs. Option A is tempting, but early hominins such as Australopithecus had small, ape-sized brains, so large brains are not the defining trait.

questions.prompt: Which group includes orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and humans, but not gibbons?
questions.explanation: Hominids are the great apes plus humans. Hominoids (option C) is tempting, but that group also includes gibbons (the lesser apes).

questions.prompt: In fossil skulls, a foramen magnum positioned centrally underneath the skull indicates that

options.A: the individual walked upright with the head balanced on top of the spine.
options.B: the individual had a large brain.

questions.explanation: A central foramen magnum means the spine joined the skull from directly below, as in an upright biped. Option B is tempting because it is a skull feature, but foramen magnum position relates to posture, not brain size.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the relationship between humans and chimpanzees is correct?

options.B: Chimpanzees are an earlier stage of human evolution.
options.C: Humans and chimpanzees share a common ancestor.
options.D: Humans and chimpanzees are not related.

questions.explanation: Both lineages descend from a common ancestor and have been evolving separately since they split. Option A is the most common misconception: living chimpanzees are cousins, not ancestors.

questions.prompt: Which change in pelvis shape is associated with bipedalism?

options.B: Pelvis angled to keep the trunk horizontal
options.C: Long pelvis that places the legs wide apart

questions.explanation: A short, wide, bowl-shaped pelvis supports the internal organs and anchors muscles that balance the body on one leg while walking. A tall, narrow pelvis (option A) is the ape condition.

questions.prompt: A skull has a cranial capacity of about 450 cm³, a projecting jaw and a central foramen magnum. The most likely classification is
questions.explanation: A small brain and prognathic face plus evidence of bipedalism fits Australopithecus. Option A is tempting because the brain size is chimp-like, but a chimpanzee would have its foramen magnum towards the back of the skull.

questions.prompt: Mitochondrial DNA shows the greatest genetic diversity among people of African descent. This supports the idea that

options.A: Homo sapiens has lived in Africa longest, so populations there have had the most time to accumulate mutations.
options.B: Homo sapiens evolved separately in many regions at once.
options.C: mitochondrial DNA mutates faster in Africa.
options.D: no migration of Homo sapiens has occurred.

questions.explanation: More diversity means more time for mutations to build up, pointing to Africa as the place of origin, consistent with the Out of Africa model. Option B is the multiregional model, which predicts diversity spread more evenly and is not supported by this pattern.

questions.prompt: Analysis of ancient DNA from Neanderthal bones compared with modern humans has shown that

options.A: Neanderthals were the direct ancestors of all modern humans.
options.B: Neanderthals and modern humans never met.
options.C: Homo sapiens interbred with Neanderthals, and many living people carry a small amount of Neanderthal DNA.
options.D: Neanderthals were a type of chimpanzee.

questions.explanation: Ancient DNA shows interbreeding left a small proportion of Neanderthal DNA in many people today. Option A is tempting, but Neanderthals were a separate lineage that shared an ancestor with us; interbreeding does not make them our direct ancestors.
